title: LLM assisted reverse engineering
lede: A hacker with two decades of hardware and software experience explains how they now reverse engineer binaries and devices by pointing an agent at the target with a small set of skills.

points: The agent identifies the binary's type and platform, then maps main functions, branching and imports, writing findings to Markdown notes that survive context compaction.
When static analysis stalls, the agent sets breakpoints, injects logging probes, or gets computer use or an emulator.
A hypothesis-debugging skill makes a stuck agent log each hypothesis in a CSV and run a decisive experiment, ending guesswork loops.
Probes are written in Python with uv and finished hacks in Rust, whose strict compiler gives the agent tight feedback.
Six months of results include custom synthesizer and e-reader firmware, mapped camera protocols and a fixed macOS printer driver.

points.text: Commenters share their own agent-assisted wins, from lighting and camera apps to CCTV plugins, children's story cartridges and audio gear.
Others recognise the guessing loops the post describes, saying Claude needs constant steering on harder targets.
A commenter who had Codex unlock paid features in Android apps draws a sharp reply calling it theft.
One reader argues that handing the work to AI removes the learning and satisfaction that make reverse engineering worth doing.
Refusals come up too: a reply says models often stonewall once the work involves reversing authentication.
